item.title: Ozempic Can Reduce Meat Consumption. But There’s A Catch
item.description: Meat CEOs are cheering on the GLP-1 boom because users eat more protein... but before-and-after shopping cart data tells a different story.
item.dc:creator: Björn
item.content:encoded:
Over the past few years, Ozempic has skyrocketed in popularity as people are drawn to these novel medicines for their ability to slim waists and reduce cravings. GLP-1 agonists like Ozempic and Wegovy reduce hunger signals to the brain and can even suppress other impulses, like gambling, shopping, or obsessively checking your Substack analytics page. But how do they affect our collective meat consumption?

Some claim GLP-1s will reduce overall consumption, including meat, while many meat-industry analysts say the increased focus on protein will boost demand for animal products. Now that the dust from the first wave of Ozempic users has settled, we’re starting to see papers on the subject, so I went looking for the numbers to settle this debate.

Good news: Ozempic will likely reduce our meat consumption… but there’s a catch. Let’s take a jab at understanding what’s really going on.

Note: I’m a sociologist, not a nutritionist. This article is a holistic review of GLP-1s’ impact on populations — nothing written in this resource should be interpreted as individual dietary advice.

Ozempic Users Eat More Meat (Sort Of)

Ozempic is the brand name for semaglutide, a drug that mimics GLP-1, a hormone your gut releases after you eat. It basically tricks your brain into feeling fuller than usual, which can help some people manage weight or diabetes. It was first approved in the U.S. in 2017, and these drugs have boomed since then — about 12% of U.S. Americans say they’re currently taking a GLP-1, and 5% of Brits say they’ve used one. [Note: throughout this piece, I’ll use “Ozempic”, “Wegovy” and “GLP-1” interchangeably.]

You might expect the meat industry to be worried about the arrival of drugs that make people eat less, but they seem to be downright ecstatic. In 2025, JBS’s CEO told investors that people on GLP-1s were adding more protein to their diets. It’s even showing up in marketing: many brands rolled out or re-marketed products in smaller sizes or emphasized meat snacks like jerky.

The meat industry is right about one thing: Ozempic users do eat more meat than the average person — in this chart, based on a 2024 meat industry study, GLP-1 users ate more of all types of meat than non-users1.

Not looking good! But some of you savvy readers might already be guessing the twist here — here’s a hint: correlation doesn’t imply causation. Think about how Ozempic users differ from the average person: they skew wealthier, more educated, and (in most surveys) more often women. Most important of all, people who take GLP-1s tend to eat more than the average person. That’s one hell of a confounder.

It’s far better to focus on a before-and-after analysis of people who do take GLP-1s. Thankfully, a new study does just that. What’s crucial about this report — very aptly titled ‘the No-Hunger Games’ — is that it measured real shopping habits at the household level.

Here, the picture is much clearer: nearly every type of animal protein is bought less often when people start taking Ozempic, especially in the first six months. Keep in mind this data is at the household level, so individual-level reductions could be even larger.

One nuance this data doesn’t show is the small-body problem. Are people swapping bigger animals (like cows and pigs) for smaller ones (like chickens and fish), which could mean more animals are raised despite overall meat reduction? The shopping data doesn’t track individual species, so I can’t say for certain, but it doesn’t seem likely. Other data suggests people on Ozempic want less of every kind of meat, including chicken and fish:

Let’s whip out some back-of-the-envelope math: If every household on Earth cut meat the way GLP-1 households do, that would mean we’d eat around 5 billion2 fewer land animals a year. Of course, it’s unlikely that everyone is going to start taking this drug, but it does show that the needle really can move the needle!

The Catch: Taste Buds Aren’t Budging

Before we get too excited, remember how Ozempic and Wegovy actually work. People who take Ozempic report experiencing less “food noise” (intrusive thoughts about eating), but many still report wanting to eat their favorite foods, including beef and chicken. That matters, because the drop in appetite is likely the main reason GLP-1 users eat less meat. Just because Ozempic users stop eating potato chips and ice cream doesn’t mean they’ve lost the taste for them.

We see this in the numbers. One cross-sectional study suggests that the desire to eat meat seems to bounce back after a year of taking a drug like Wegovy.

So everything hinges on what happens when people stop taking the drug. Remember that study that tracked real-world shopping habits? Well, they also tracked what happened to the third of participants who quit using the drug during the study period. Across every meat and animal-product category, their purchases went back to roughly pre-drug levels.

The meat reduction holds up well while people stay on the drug. Once the jabs stop, the appetite comes roaring back. And plenty of people stop: different studies put the one-year drop-off at 40%, 50%, and 68%.

There’s also a psychological reason the change doesn’t stick. I’ve argued before that values tend to follow behavior: once people eat less meat, they start to see themselves as the kind of person who eats less meat. But psychologists have known since the 1960s that this only works when people feel responsible for the change, not when they credit a drug or a placebo. Ozempic users face the same trap. If someone eats half as much steak because a weekly injection made the thought of eating it nauseating, they’ll probably attribute their behavior change to the drug, not to themselves. This makes it harder for them to maintain any changes once the drug stops coming.

Like this analysis? Subscribe now to get resources like these in your inbox. Always free, never spam.

From Wegovy to ‘We Go Vegan’

So, while Wegovy does make people eat less meat and animal products, it’s far from a death knell for Big Meat. But GLP-1s create a massive advantage we’d be wise not to pass up: a cohort of people eating less meat than before.

Taking Ozempic creates something called a habit disruption window — a period when your context changes and you are more susceptible to changing your habits than you normally would be. It’s why people who move to a new city are more likely to swap out their car for a bike commute, and why, the week I started university, I decided to dye my hair bright blue and purple.

Habit disruption windows are rare for diet change. A 2018 analysis found that neither marriage, divorce, kids leaving home, nor salary bumps predicted any change in diet. The only thing that was able to make a dent was a diabetes diagnosis, and even that barely budged people’s habits. So it’s exciting that something like Ozempic can meaningfully change meat consumption habits, if only temporarily.

We need to figure out a way to change people’s habits before the habit disruption window closes entirely. Evidence suggests this can work: in a Danish study, people who took and then stopped liraglutide (an older GLP-1 drug) regained 6 kg, while those who also built an exercise routine regained only 2.5 kg.

In other words, using the Wegovy window to change habits might make the consumption change last longer. For meat reduction, this means the first few months of a GLP-1 are key to helping people find plant-based meals they enjoy and a community that helps them stick to new habits.

One way this could work is by introducing them to high-quality alternative proteins. Some evidence suggests that Wegovy users are more willing to pay higher prices for alternative proteins, but only in retail settings, not in restaurants.

Price alone won’t sell alternative protein, but I suspect alt-protein companies would be wise to ride the protein craze in the supermarket aisle, like Beyond’s pivot to protein waters or Vemondo’s plant-based protein puddings. There’s probably a big market for plant-based protein snacks, like protein bars, vegan jerky, soy yogurts, and other smaller items.

Closing the Window

GLP-1s will likely reduce meat consumption, at least in the short term, but the effect won’t be enough to move meat companies’ bottom lines, and it’s unlikely to turn anyone vegan overnight.

The bigger opportunity is the window to change habits more permanently. For the first six months or so of taking these drugs, millions of people across the world are eating less meat without consciously trying to. That’s rare. We don’t normally see dietary changes spread so fast, even if they’re as short-lived as this one. If advocates and alt-protein companies can connect new Wegovy users with plant-based meal swaps they actually enjoy, and help them feel the change is coming from within, this short-term reduction might stick around when the medicine stops.

1

Notably, the number of people who eat alternative protein doesn’t change much (although the study authors counted eggs as “alternative proteins,” which basically makes the category meaningless anyway).

2

The FAO estimated that about 88 billion land animals were slaughtered for meat in 2024. GLP-1 households cut meat spending by 5.2–5.6%, which is roughly 4.6–4.9 billion animals out of 88 billion. These figures assume spending cuts translate one-to-one into animals and that cuts are spread evenly across species. Since most animals killed are chickens, the real number depends heavily on whether chicken purchases fall as much as other meats.

item.title: I Built a Calculator to Measure Your Nudge Impact
item.description: With the Better Food Foundation, I created a new tool to help advocates strategize better about plant-based nudges.
item.dc:creator: Björn
item.content:encoded:
Most of my writing focuses on strategy — what policies are best, what messaging tactics will actually change someone’s mind, and how we can build the meat reduction movement at scale. Today, I have something new to share with you: a resource you can use to convince someone to actually create large-scale change.

I’m excited to show you the Plant-Based Nudge Calculator, a fresh, interactive tool I developed1 with the Better Food Foundation. For the first time, advocates can estimate how many animal-based meals their local institution can replace with plant-based nudges — useful for impact analysis, strategy, and advocacy alike. Here’s how it works.

What Are Plant-Based Nudges?

The basics: a plant-based nudge changes how food is presented to maximize the chances someone orders an animal-free meal, without removing meat as an option. A vegan restaurant isn’t a nudge, since the customer doesn’t have a choice of eating meat. Changing menu language or making vegan food the default option? Both are nudges.

The idea is that if we meet people where they are, we can influence more people to eat plant-based. Instead of asking one person at a time to change, plant-based nudges focus on changing the environments in which we eat, not the diners themselves. Want to learn more? Check out my resources on the topic here. If you’re an advocate looking to use them more in your work, I’d strongly recommend attending the Better Food Foundation’s free Nudge Trainings.

How the Calculator Works

The Plant-Based Nudge Calculator is exactly what it sounds like. You plug in a few basic numbers about a dining setting — meals served per day, days open per year, customers per day — pick one of five research-backed nudges, and it spits out two estimates: how many meals shift from animal-based to plant-based over a year, and how much CO₂e that shift saves.

To put it into practice, imagine a campus dining hall (a classic place to implement a plant-based nudge). It serves 2 meals a day to 2,000 students around roughly 250 times a year. If you were to implement a plant-based default here, the research suggests you’d save 496,500 animal-based meals2 a year and nearly nine hundred thousand kilograms of carbon emissions.

“[The nudge calculator is] an immensely valuable, simple tool to help people to see what they can accomplish, and how they can achieve their goals.” — Cass R. Sunstein, Harvard University, BFF Board of Advisors, Co-Author of Nudge and writer of

The best way to understand this tool is to use it! Check it out: I suggest picking a local food service location and seeing how many meals you can change. Might be more or less than you think!

Try it now!

How I Built It

To build a tool like this, I first categorized all of the various nudge studies I’ve been reading over the years into BFF’s Top Five Nudges. For each nudge, I created a multiplier by averaging the percentage-point increases across studies (except for ratios, which required a regression equation). I focused on absolute change (e.g., “vegan food went from being ordered 5% of the time to 18% of the time”) instead of relative change (e.g., “a 50% increase in plant-based food sales”).

This tool is a snapshot of the current research. I don’t view advocacy science as static, so think of this tool as our best available estimate, one that may change in the future as research comes out. I made sure to add in a confidence estimate for each nudge category — a somewhat subjective assessment of how strong the evidence is for each group. In some cases, advocates may have access to food procurement data, which would show more accurate estimates3.

In the future, I am interested in adding new features if novel research comes out. Especially longitudinal studies or research into interaction effects between nudges. Stay tuned for more updates!

Why I Am Excited About It

Look, I get it. I’m a data nerd who’s excited about developing a calculator. Fork found in kitchen.

But bear with me: now, dining hall directors can calculate the exact amount of emissions they could save by implementing a nudge. Before, say, a university dining hall director would have had to either 1. rely on general information, 2. aggregate tons of procurement data to sift through, or 3. do lots of academic research themselves, which no one has time for. Now, they can spend two minutes figuring out the best way to incentivize plant-based options while staying in line with their sustainability goals. Even better, advocates can make conversations with food service managers go as smooth as plant-based butter.

The hardest part about being a meat reduction advocate usually isn’t convincing someone to change their mind, but to align their actions with their values. Making a big change creates friction. This tool is designed to reduce that friction by taking hard work off of food service managers’ plates to make the transition a bit easier. Sometimes, that’s the difference between a successful implementation and a failed one.

I sincerely hope this helps make it easier to implement plant-based nudges worldwide! If you plan to use this tool, you can share feedback here.

Where did the Idea Come from?

Sometimes, to create tools like this, people need time to experiment, tinker with ideas, write off-kilter posts, and bark up some weird trees. In my case, the nudge calculator came from a series of posts I did last year about the data behind nudges. While writing those posts, I began to see new ways to categorize nudges by their absolute change, so I could better synthesize studies. The great folks at the Better Food Foundation then helped me translate these ideas from my brain’s whiteboard into the real world.

That’s one reason I find this Substack valuable — not only do I get to create exciting resources for the advocacy community, but it also gives me the freedom to try things out before they’re perfectly ready. So I also want to acknowledge all of you — especially the folks who’ve been subscribing (and especially paid subscribers) to More Than Meats the Eye from the jump! Please pat yourselves on the back — this tool couldn’t have existed without you.

Feedback? Take a two-minute survey here

If you like stuff like this and want to see more of my ideas about how to fix meat consumption, consider sharing, subscribing, or even becoming a paid subscriber. Your support makes it a helluva lot easier for me to think deeper into the issues, come up with original ideas, and build tools like this that can improve our world:

Subscribe now

1

With a major assist from Claude Code, of course.

2

I’ve also created a way to add animal lives represented by the switch from animal-based to plant-based foods. You can find those multipliers here.

3

If you want to tailor the calculations to your institution, especially large institutions, we can make the estimations even more precise. Email me at bjorn@betterfoodfoundation.org, and I can see what we can do.

item.title: Why Telling People How Bad Factory Farming Is Doesn't Always Work
item.description: According to brand-new polling data, nearly everyone underestimates factory farming's scale. But correcting them isn’t always the best move. Here’s why.
item.dc:creator: Björn
item.content:encoded:
Today, I published a report on what the public really thinks about factory farming, and it has changed how I view our messaging strategies.

The report, written in collaboration with Laila Kassam and Natalie Braine from Project Phoenix, is based on a survey of 2,000 people in the UK to better understand their views on factory farming. What we found was pretty optimistic! Two-thirds of Brits say that factory farming is wrong or raises moral concerns, 54% want it ended or phased out (not just regulated), and a slim majority (51%) think we should all be eating a lot less meat.

Read the full report here!

While I was reviewing the data, one number kept sticking in my brain. We asked everyone what percentage of animals in the UK they thought were factory-farmed. 96% of respondents either underestimated the number or had no idea.

My first thought when I saw this massive knowledge chasm was the most obvious: correct it. Just tell people how bad it really is, and we’re halfway to solving the problem! It’s an instinctive and natural reaction that I had — but it’s also dead wrong.

The Problem of Scale

In 1992, back when The Bodyguard was dominating the box office, researchers ran what would become an infamous study in donor psychology. People read a story about migratory birds drowning in uncovered oil ponds and were asked how much they’d pay to prevent it. Simple enough. The catch was that different people saw different numbers of affected birds — 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000. It made almost no difference in how the three groups chose to donate: $80, $78, and $88, respectively.

It’s been replicated many times since, swapping in different victims — refugees, farmed animals — creating a clear pattern: as the scale of a problem increases, our concern for it barely budges. We are all scope-insensitive.

There’s a reason our brains work this way. If we took the grief we feel for one suffering person and multiplied it by a million, our minds short-circuit — drowning in despair, fear, and helplessness. Instead, we undergo psychic numbing, an empathetic defense mechanism, which makes it harder for us to understand and act on big issues, like genocide, climate change, and of course, factory farming.

Factory farming is really, really, really bad, and really, really, really big: it affects billions of land animals every year and trillions when we count aquatic animals too. I often see animal advocates posting these factory farming statistics, hoping it’ll shock people into taking action. I get the instinct. But “billions of chickens are suffering right now” plopped onto an Instagram carousel, with no story attached, may actually do the opposite.

Statistics can work — here are the three ways I think are most strategic.

Get People Calculating, Not Just Feeling

The first strategy comes from a study my old behavioral science lab ran in 2004 (well before my time, so I can’t take any credit) that examined how our mindsets affect rational thinking.

The researchers primed participants to either think in a logical, calculating way (by making them do math problems) or an emotional way (by making them explain their feelings related to certain words). Then, they gave them another task, which they thought was unrelated: evaluating the cost of either 5 or 10 Madonna CDs. It turned out that the state of mind someone was in before making this evaluation was crucial: the thinkers valued the CDs more rationally, i.e., they valued 10 CDs as roughly double 5 CDs. But the feelers didn’t. They judged the groups of CDs as worth about the same. The paper replicated the idea three times in different domains: people who think in a calculated way judge the value of numbers more accurately than people who think emotionally.

If this all seems like mumbo-jumbo, think of it this way: feeling is an on-off switch: we either care about the Madonna CDs or we don’t. Calculation is a sliding scale: we are more sensitive to increases in value and rate it proportionately.

To help people to better understand the scale of factory farming, we need to get them into a calculating state of mind, not a feeling one. Easier said than done — we can’t exactly walk up to strangers and hand them multiplication tables, now can we?

Instead, we can catch them when they’re already making comparative evaluations. When we compare two or more options — say, which charity on a list to donate to — we are more likely to take scale into account, likely because our minds are primed for these types of calculations. But if we are only looking at one option, the problem of scale comes back. Researchers call these joint evaluation and single evaluation, respectively.

Most pro-animal actions are single evaluations. People don’t sit down and weigh the pros and cons of various diets — they think about whether veganism is right for them. Other scenarios do involve joint evaluations: choosing your next job or career, picking a charity to donate to on a non-profit evaluator, or choosing an investment portfolio that doesn’t invest in factory farming. This is when statistics are most likely to be convincing.

Never Show the Problem Without a Solution

Why aren’t more people changing their diets? In 2022, researchers at Pax Fauna interviewed dozens of meat-eaters to pop the hood on the underlying psychological resistance to meat reduction. They found a predictable sequence in their interviewees: avoidance, guilt, then lots of justifications. If you read my piece on cognitive dissonance, the various rationalizations — humans won’t stop eating meat; there is no ethical consumption under capitalism — shouldn’t be too surprising. They all appealed to a sense of futility. If you can’t solve the issue, why bother even trying?

The Pax Fauna research taps into a psychological concept known as pseudoinefficacy: seeing individuals we can’t help makes us feel bad, even outweighing the warmth we feel from helping others. If we toss one starfish into the sea, we’re still going to be bummed out seeing all the ones we couldn’t help. For many, this prevents taking any action at all.

To beat that futility, we need to provide a scalable solution, ideally one the person can contribute to themselves. This works best when their action is directly linked to the solution, like when a citizen votes for an anti-factory farming ballot initiative or a dining director decides to implement a plant-based default in their cafeteria.

For someone who doesn’t have institutional power to stop factory farming (which is most of us), we’ll need to use other methods of persuasion. Dynamic social norms — where we communicate the momentum of a solution — are one possibility. That would involve saying something like “plant-based eating is the fastest-growing dietary pattern in our country.”

People are more likely to absorb the scale of the problem when they believe they are well-placed to actually help fix it.

Shrink The Problem

Humans are weird sometimes. We respond more positively when we can solve a greater chunk of a problem, regardless of the raw number of individuals we’ve managed to help. We grab onto percentages, not raw numbers, even though the number of individuals helped is what actually matters. Sometimes, we will even choose to help fewer people (100 out of 200) if it’s a larger percentage of the people in need than another group (120 out of 1,000). That’s wild!

If you tell people they can save 200 animals — a rounding error in the grand scheme of the world’s farming systems — they’ll just shrug. But if they can save 200 out of 250 animals, they’ll be more likely to jump into action. Here’s what it can look like in practical terms: some stats about local factory farms — “there are four factory farms in our district, so let’s unite to convert them,” feels a hell of a lot more doable than “there are 80 billion chickens suffering in the world, so eat some cauliflower hot wings.”

It’s also one reason why I suspect the Ridglan farm rescue succeeded — because so few animals were involved, people felt they had a real chance of making a change for them and were thus more motivated to take action.

We have a psychological predisposition for picking low-hanging fruit, so let’s use that to our advantage.

How To Make the Numbers Work for You

The knowledge gap about factory farming is very, very real. But simply telling people about how big the problem is won’t move them to act. As tempting as it is to shout big, scary statistics into the void, we need to be smarter than that.

It’s best to only communicate the immense scale of factory farming when people are A. already thinking in a logical and comparative way (like when they’re choosing from a list of charities), B. well-placed to work on a solution (like for important stakeholders or during a key vote), or C. seeing the problem shrunk down to feel more solvable (like in a local campaign).

If we can’t do one of these things, it’s probably best to skip the statistics entirely and simply get people to care about a specific animal. You are probably familiar with the phrase “one death is a tragedy, one million is a statistic.” It’s true. We are more likely to feel empathy for a single individual than for a group, including a group of animals.

The Project Phoenix report is full of numbers, but we need to communicate them effectively. Lead with the ones that build momentum — like how a majority of Brits are opposed to or concerned about factory farming — and only mention the problem’s scale when people are ready to calculate, act, or shrink the problem down to size.

The facts are on our side. Let’s use them strategically.

Before you go

Like learning practical, evidence-based lessons to make your advocacy more effective? That’s exactly why I write More Than Meats The Eye — behavioral research translated into strategy you can actually use. It’s free, and always will be.

item.title: Being Right isn’t Enough to Go Viral. Here’s What Is.
item.description: The AI-water myth went everywhere. Here's a new framework to make true facts about factory farming do the same.
item.dc:creator: Björn
item.content:encoded:
In my last post, I explored how people’s anger about AI data centers is disproportionately high compared to the water waste from factory farming. This myth isn’t the only environmental statement that punched above its weight class — remember that summer when we all collectively decided to ban plastic straws to save the oceans? Yeah, plastic straws, those little buggers that make up less than 0.03% of the plastic being dumped into the seas? Or gas stoves? Or ‘save the bees’?

We’ve all been through this song-and-dance before. There will always be some stat or narrative that breaks into the mainstream despite being super misleading, distracting, or just outright wrong. Bemoaning this phenomenon isn’t going to stop it. Instead, I would rather think critically about fact transmission so we can apply these lessons to meat reduction.

To do so, I went looking for what actually makes a fact travel. Here’s what I found.

The Facts are on Our Side. No One Cares.

Despite decades of narrative work from animal rights and climate groups, people still have completely misinformed ideas of the reality of animal agriculture. Most people just don’t really understand the scale of the issue we are dealing with, arguably the largest moral catastrophe on Earth today:

Even more frustrating than the lack of awareness is blatant misinformation that has seeped into the public consciousness: that vegan leather is greenwashing, that “ultra-processed” is a meaningful food category, that eating local matters more than eating plant-based, that regenerative ag is a scalable solution, that soy raises estrogen — take your pick.

Stopping these ‘zombie facts’ feels like a Sisyphean game of whack-a-mole. First of all, fact-checking takes forever: it takes way longer to correct a falsehood than to invent one, something I know all too well after spending hours crunching data in my previous post. Secondly, being fact-checked doesn’t always update people’s knowledge — and when it does, it might not change their underlying feelings towards the issue. Sometimes people cede the fact but not the argument1, even if the fact was load-bearing. And people just don’t like being fact-checked and often avoid information that might correct them.

Debunking falsehoods is playing defense. Important, yes, but we’re ceding an entire narrative arena to our opponents instead of seeding the ground with better-chosen facts:

The Four Vs of Virality

In 2015, researchers ran a scientific game of telephone: they showed people urban legends chock-full of eye-catching details: think spiders, steroids, cybersex, indecent exposure, and serial killers. Each person wrote a summary of the story, then handed that summary to the next person, who did the exact same thing, and on it went. The researchers then studied how the stories changed as they were retold. Unsurprisingly, lots of nuance was stripped away, like how, in one story, the word “apparently” vanished entirely, making an important point into a hardened fact instead of a guess.

Experiments like these help us to understand what types of facts are likely to persist over time and which ones fade away into obscurity. After reading a bunch of these papers, I’ve created a framework for understanding what types of facts are ripe for virality:

1. Voltage — does it spike the right emotions?

  • Poses a threat, ideally to the reader or their community

  • Involves disgust: contamination, bodies, or food

  • Evokes a high-arousal2 emotion like fear, disgust, anger

2. Villain — does it create an in-group and out-group?

  • Names a them, a face to blame

  • Stays social — about people, norms, who did what to whom

  • Makes the sharer look smart, moral, in-the-know, or otherwise improves their reputation

3. Velcro — will they remember and repeat it?

  • Breaks one rule of how the world works — one rule, not ten

  • Rides on a round, simple number that survives a retelling (”ten miles,” “90%”)

4. Veneer — will they believe it?

  • Goes down easy — claims that are simple to process feel truer, and truer still each time they’re repeated

  • Feels novel to the audience

  • Picks up a citable-looking source early

From this list, it’s easy to see why the AI-water myth caught fire: it has a clear claim that survives a game of telephone (“one bottle of water is one AI email”), that makes people angry, feel threatened, and has a clear villain: Big Tech. It doesn’t hurt that it’s a form of high-brow misinformation that grants people status for sharing it.

At first glance, many animal ag stats should also fit these criteria. Here’s how I think we can frame them better to make them really stick.

Picking Facts That Stick

Voltage: Forget Sadness, Choose Anger

Contrary to Inside Out, sadness might actually be overrated. Many narratives around animal welfare evoke low-arousal emotions like sadness, when stories around anger are more likely to proliferate. I suspect this is because many activists are themselves driven by grief and empathy, so they spread stories that resonate with them. But sad stories of a chicken with an injured leg don’t go viral.

Remember the story of Cedar the goat — the poor animal who was unjustly stolen from her human and subsequently killed and eaten? Or Cecil the lion or Peanut the squirrel or Freya the walrus or Harambe the gorilla? These stories went everywhere, due in part to how god-damn angry they make you feel3. High-energy emotions trump low-energy ones every time.

  • Invoke fear: 70% of medically important antibiotics in the U.S. go to farmed animals, fueling concerns about antibiotic resistance

  • Stoke disgust: fast-growth breeding has left the vast majority of supermarket chicken breasts with muscle disorders like white striping and “woody breast”

  • Make people angry: people living near concentrated animal feeding operations face documented respiratory problems

Villain: Give Big Meat a Face

Quick, can you name the CEO of a meat company? I’d bet no4. But I’m 100% confident you can name an AI CEO or executive: Sam Altman, Jensen Huang, or Elon Musk come to mind pretty easily.

We should all act more like reality TV producers and cast villains. A “them” turns meat-eaters into an “us,” and gives the movement something to recruit against rather than someone to scold. This also solves another problem for virality: conveying status to the fact-sharer. A major problem in animal advocacy is that merely talking about the issues transforms you into a “preachy vegan” and makes people resent you. By explicitly naming an out-group, you may be able to foster solidarity and gain trust.

I don’t think this should be too difficult really — these CEOs ain’t no saints. The meat industry5 is filled with stories of corrupt officials employing children on slaughterhouse floors illegally, bribing politicians, fixing prices, breaking anti-trust laws, and even betting on which employees would get sick from COVID-19. I often read meat industry blogs and news articles, so I counted how many of them reference some sort of scandal or issue that would generate negative press6. Of the 1,000 articles I reviewed, 300 referenced a scandal or problem — and this is on their own blog posts. Here are the types of things they mentioned:

Velcro: Take One Fact Off

Animal agriculture is terrible in basically every way a thing can be terrible. Bad for the planet, bad for animals, bad for the economy, bad for pandemic risk, bad for human health, bad for workers’ rights… It’s just bad, full stop. But this is more of a curse than a blessing, because it creates a narrative that’s too difficult to stick in your brain.

If you had to explain an animal ag story to your aunt (while she’s three lemon spritzers deep into a family dinner), could she repeat it the next day? Most of our best facts wouldn’t: they’re accurate but forgettable. “Regardless of the way it’s produced, beef has a substantially higher lifecycle emissions profile than plant protein, even more if you count land use change” is something that’ll slip away the second dessert is served. But “a single burger emits the same as driving ten miles” might just stick around.

To paraphrase Coco Chanel — before you publish the report, take one fact off. One thing I like about the recent Project Slingshot campaigns is how each one centers around a single concept. Their launch campaign, “I Don’t Buy It,” runs on essentially one line: 90% of pigs in the UK are slaughtered in CO2 gas chambers. Now we’re talking. This is the type of thing that has the potential to survive in your brain long enough to go viral.

Veneer: Make It Feel New

In a study of Twitter misinformation, the factor the researchers zeroed in on as the biggest predictor of why false news outran the truth was how novel it felt. Crucially, novelty is subjective — something that might feel stale to you may feel brand-new to the general public.

To prioritize novelty, we need to understand our audience’s perceptions of the issues. Some underexplored angles that might land as brand-new: that the shrimp industry blinds its breeding females to make them spawn, how we kill birds with heatstroke to prevent bird flu, or that nearly every chicken on Earth descends from two companies’ genetics. More research into the salience of these facts would certainly help us select them better.

Things that are always novel are about current events: this is one of the reasons I think opposition to the ”Save Our Bacon Act” got so strong; this is a current, fresh issue instead of a well-trodden debate about welfare. So whenever you see an animal issue in the mainstream, latch onto it to ride its novelty.

Time to Let the Truth Travel

The facts are on our side. It’s undeniably true that billions of individuals are suffering in animal factories, that animal agriculture is polluting our land and rivers, and that moving away from an animal-based food system would reap benefits for our health. Our problem has never been a shortage of damning facts. It’s that we keep presenting them like a lab report and expecting them to resonate like a scandal.

Instead of throwing everything against a wall and seeing what sticks, we can use our understanding of virality to carefully select facts that are more likely to break into the mainstream. Plenty of disinformation or highly misleading stats have done so already — it’s high time we start playing the same game.

Like learning about how to change our food systems? Subscribe to get these resources straight in your inbox. Always free, no spam:

1

In one study, people told a piece of information was false kept leaning on it anyway — reasoning as if the correction never landed, even when they could recite it back to you. It’s called the continued influence effect. Studies on politicians and immigration show corrections fix the facts but not the feelings: fact-checked voters came away with more accurate beliefs, yet their support for the candidate — and their views on the policy — didn’t budge.

2

“arousal” in this context means more excited or energetic, not, like, horny

3

And, in the case of Harambe, lots of memes.

4

Unless you’re a professional campaigner, that is, of whom I’m guessing plenty exist in my audience. But the underlying point is still true that the general public certainly couldn’t.

5

While researching this piece, I tried to find data about the approval rating of Big Meat companies — but, to my knowledge, this polling doesn’t exist. Likely because most people think of Tyson as a product, not as a company. That’s a pretty big research gap in my opinion — if we want people to view Big Meat the same way they view Big Oil or Big Tech, we need to be asking those questions.

6

Meatingplace is trade press — written for the meat industry, by people broadly friendly to it. So I wanted to know how often its own pages still read as bad news. Over eight months it ran 1,000 General News stories; I read every one and flagged the 300 that a reporter or campaigner could turn against the industry. Here’s what those 300 are made of. The surprise is what sits at the bottom: animal welfare, the beat you’d expect to fill an animal-advocacy inbox, is the smallest slice at 4%. The industry’s real reputational exposure comes from disease and recalls (31%), antitrust and fraud litigation (25%), and how it treats the people on the line (17%).

item.title: AI Isn't Draining the Rivers. Your Dinner Is.
item.description: The real story of AI's water footprint, the animal-agriculture comparison no one makes, and how one bad stat went viral.
item.dc:creator: Björn
item.content:encoded:
I knocked over a full glass of water about four paragraphs into writing this piece. That moment of clumsiness used more water than every question I’ve asked Claude to research the whole post — and almost certainly more than my entire month of AI use. But here’s the thing: if we actually cared about water, we’d look at the dinner table, where a single meatloaf matters orders of magnitude more than a lifetime of chatting up Chat.

And then the mystery that really gets me: how did a stat this shaky seep so deep into the zeitgeist — and what do we do about it?

Animal Factories Use Way More Water Than AI. Like, Way More

AI doesn’t really use that much water. I won’t harp on this point too much (mostly because it’s already been covered in more depth by ), but here’s a brief overview: a ChatGPT query’s full water footprint is roughly 0.9 mL — about two teardrops — and ~85% of that is offsite at the power plant, not the cooling tower everyone pictures.

But there is an industry that does gulp down water like there’s no tomorrow: animal factories. Globally, animal agriculture uses over a quarter of the freshwater we use, and the water use of animal products is always higher than that of the best nutritionally equivalent plant-based options. Now, when people hear this, they might picture cows and pigs and chickens in a field tossing back water like Robert Hays on an airplane, but most of this water, 98%, is actually from animal feed. This is a recurring theme when analyzing the environmental hoofprint of animal ag — we have to include all the inputs for the animal feed as well, which tends to be plants like corn, soy, and alfalfa, which all need water for themselves. If instead we used that land to grow food for humans, we’d be able to save a ton of water.

How big is this difference? Massive. I charted the water use of a few animal-based and plant-based foods, along with the usage of 10,0001 AI prompts. To be extra fair, I plotted both the highest and lowest estimates of AI water usage I could find2.

And remember, this is compared against 10,000 AI prompts, which would still take well over a month, even for the hardest-core Claude fan. Swapping out just one beef burger for an Heura burger saves about as much water as vibe-coding to your heart’s desire3.

This argument holds up even if we examine the water use by type. Quick refresher: green water is rainwater soaked into soil and transpired by plants, while blue water is the more important metric: the surface and groundwater we actively pull from rivers and reservoirs. Still, the underlying facts stand if we look at just blue water: 10,000 prompts, which is roughly enough for a year’s use, is still, at the very highest estimate, worth 2 kilos of tofu (or, as I call it, a serving size). No matter how you cut it, your food choices matter more than your AI.

But let’s flip the way we look at it. What about from a national perspective, in terms of a nation’s total water usage? This is where the problem really starts to look absurd — animal agriculture is the single largest use of water, responsible for over 40%! That’s more than every shower, golf course, jacuzzi, slip ‘n slide, factory, faucet, swimming pool, sprinkler, toilet, water park, and TikTok rug cleaning video combined.

This gap is probably far higher in other developed countries — consider how the US is a net importer of beef and has an above-average number of data centers. The USA likely has the smallest ratio of animal agriculture’s water use to data centers’... and it’s still a factor of 130.

Many people would also argue that even though AI’s water usage is small in aggregate, it’s concentrated where it hurts. This is somewhat defensible. Estimates vary from 32% to 66% of data centers that are built or planned in areas of high water stress.

But let’s apply the same logic to factory farming and animal feed. Ceres found that 35% of global-corn-based feed is grown in regions of high or extremely high water stress. Zoom out to rivers and it gets worse. Livestock farming alone pushes 7% of the world’s rivers past the freshwater planetary boundary, and in another 34% it would blow past that boundary even if every other industry vanished. This is a far worse problem because there are way more animal farms than data centers. Again, orders of magnitude worse. This is a real problem, and I hope local ordinances get better at protecting the specific communities located near data centers and factory farms.

“We find irrigation of cattle-feed crops to be the greatest consumer of river water in the western United States, implicating beef and dairy consumption as the leading driver of water shortages and fish imperilment in the region.” — Richter et al., Nature Sustainability (2020)

The Villain Edit, In Numbers

It’s a pretty open-and-shut case: when it comes to water usage, animal agriculture is a far bigger threat than data centers. But no one seems to believe it. It feels like every single conversation nowadays irrevocably circles back to the idea of wasting water – something that never seems to happen when we’re munching on hamburgers.

But you know me, feeling vibes isn’t actually enough to be sure. So I sat down and counted. I pulled about 400 water-and-industry stories from nine big US and UK papers — the Post, the Journal, the Guardian, and similar outlets — from July 2024 through June 2026, and read each one to see when they mentioned AI or Animal agriculture as a threat4. Here’s what I found:

AI gets framed as a threat to water roughly a third of the time. Animal agriculture? Only about one story in twenty. Toggle between the two tabs to see just how disproportionate this coverage actually is — you are nearly six times more likely to see an article about AI’s water use in a mainstream paper even though animal farms drink up 130 times more water. Oof.

While this data doesn’t come from a preregistered study, it maps nearly perfectly onto existing data. Several outlets and researchers have estimated that only a very small percentage — 1.5%, 3.6%, 3.8%, 4%, and 7% — of climate stories mention animal agriculture. My 6.7% figure sits nicely within that range.

It gets worse when I examined the type of coverage. Animal farms are usually portrayed as victims: stories where drought shrinks the herd, ranchers cull5 their animals, or your breakfast McMuffin gets more expensive. AI, meanwhile, gets the villain edit — “your cloud is drying my river,” as one Spanish activist put it.

If you don’t believe me, run the experiment yourself. Go to any social media site, search “AI water use,” then search “animal agriculture water use,” and start scrolling. It won’t take long before you see what I mean.

Anatomy of a Faulty Stat

This is…strange, no? I’d argue that a switch away from data centers, or an extreme reduction in their use, would change the fabric of industrialized society far more than swapping from animal-based to plant-based foods. Would you rather eat soy-based chicken nuggets and oat milk lattes or have to send carrier pigeons instead of DMs for the rest of your life? It’s worth investigating where exactly this all came from.

The viral “one email, one bottle of water” claim started with a genuine 2023 preprint: half a liter for a whole conversation of 10–50 prompts on GPT-3. Then, in September 2024, the Washington Post wrote up that data into a fancy infographic, where the idea started to make a splash. Funnily enough, that original post argued that training GPT3 used the same amount of water as the amount of beef two US Americans eat in a year. But this caveat only appeared at the very end of the piece, and readers didn’t seem to put the water usage of AI into that perspective — only the “one bottle of water” claim stuck.

From there, it spread like wildfire (you know wildfire, the stuff that animal agriculture is fueling). Tom’s Hardware put the worst case in the headline (three bottles!), a news TikTok with over a million likes carried it further, and Snopes, an actual fact-checking site, repeated it without much scrutiny. By 2026, Claude’s water use had clawed its way into becoming folk belief, beyond any attempt at numeracy. Some say that writing "please" and "thank you" to a chatbot is an act of environmental vandalism. TikTok is full of vague water-use claims. Brands are slapping it on billboards. Politicians are capitalizing on it. Millions of people now feel a small pang of ecological guilt over an amount of liquid that couldn’t even water a houseplant.

The punchline is that the researcher who produced the original figure has since walked it back to roughly 15 mL for GPT-4. This correction, needless to say, has not gone viral.

Like this analysis? Subscribe to get it in your inbox, for free:

So What Do We Do With This?

I have two conflicting feelings seeing a fact like this spread so rapidly. First, and most obvious, the data scientist part of my brain is recoiling in horror at seeing some “alternative facts” slowly become part of the zeitgeist. It is unbelievably frustrating to see genuine political power6 rally around a low-key environmental villain when that energy could instead go towards fighting the number one cause of deforestation across the world.

But there’s another part of me that’s sitting up and paying attention. If a narrative like this can come out of seemingly nowhere — based on facts that crumble apart as easily as Nature Valley bars — what’s stopping us from doing the same thing7?

Part 2 of this story — where I will analyze what types of facts tend to go viral, and what we need to learn from them — is available here:

Read Part 2 Now

1

I chose 10,000 so you could actually see the color on the chart — I first tried it with 1,000 and the bar was literally invisible.

2

These two estimates differ in both who researched them and whether they calculated indirect water usage as well.

3

To be clear, this doesn’t mean that AI is inherently perfect. There are valid criticisms against AI — how deepfakes can spread misinformation, potential job losses in some fields, the risk of cyberattacks, misuse of personal data, etc. — but water usage just isn’t one of them.

4

This data absolutely isn’t a formal research study, but I modeled it after best practices in the field, including studies by Sentient Media and some of my previous research into media landscapes.

5

Remind that “cull” is an industry word for “kill,” often without any painkillers or pain-mitigation techniques.

6

Again, I think political pressure on AI can absolutely be a good thing. Work or social programs to help people at risk of losing their jobs, restrictions on AI companies selling data, and similar policies would all be good ideas! But broadly banning data centers because of shoddy stats isn’t.

7

After all, the facts are on OUR side.

item.title: We've Been Looking for Pre-Vegans in the Wrong Places
item.description: What a six-month Te Protejo report I worked on reveals about who's actually ready for diet change
item.dc:creator: Björn
item.content:encoded:
Many of us have a standard playbook for identifying who’s ready to change their diet: segment by diet stage (omnivore, flexitarian, vegetarian, vegan) and target the middle, because they’re the ones most responsive to advocacy tactics. Rinse, wash, repeat. But I’ve recently conducted a study that has made me question this framework: maybe we need to think beyond the idea of flexitarians as pre-vegans and consider other groups as well.

To help answer this question, we may need to look not at the dinner table, but in our bathroom cabinets.

I Ran a Six-Month Study. Here’s What Surprised Me.

When I’m not writing Substack posts, I’m writing research reports1. Last week, I published a new report commissioned from Te Protejo to evaluate the success of their new program, Tu Compromiso Cruelty-Free (“Your Cruelty-Free Commitment”). The six-month program provided participants curious about cruelty-free2 (CF) cosmetics with structured resources, including practical guides, webinars, community groups, and curated educational materials about vegan foods, clothes, and makeup brands. Think Veganuary, targeted at women in Latin America, and about cruelty-free products as well.

To measure impact, I sent out surveys at three points — before, midway through, and after the program — to 539 participants who consistently engaged with program materials. And the program was a success! Participants significantly reduced their animal product consumption, with several flexitarians and vegetarians becoming fully vegan by the end of the six-month period. My calculations indicate that program participants are now eating 65 fewer pigs, 163 fewer chickens, 78 fewer fish, and half a cow less annually.

I’ve written extensively about diet challenges before — I’ve found that they tend to convert 10% to 28% of participants to long-term dietary change and that they’re optimal for converting people who are already a few steps along the “vegan pipeline”. The same was true for the Cruelty-Free challenge: about 30% of participants were vegan at the start of the program, and 70%3 reported buying only Cruelty-Free cosmetics.

But here’s the thing that really stuck with me: none of the demographic details I tested — age, country, motivations — predicted who would succeed in the Tu Compromiso program. But there was something that did: people who entered the program already buying cruelty-free cosmetics exclusively were more than twice as likely4 to be vegan by the end — 45.2% versus 21.7%.

This really surprised me. I expected that initial motivations especially would predict success, or maybe one’s country. This finding sent me down a rabbit hole (don’t worry, the rabbit was cruelty-free). If CF buyers are twice as likely to go vegan, how many of them are actually out there?

The Market Nobody Thought to Count

Just like in determining the real number of vegans in the world, it’s hard to tell how many women are cruelty-free. To help get to the bottom of it, I charted all the surveys that asked about it here:

As we can see, the numbers vary quite a bit — especially given that the survey questions asked about both current and hypothetical purchases. Another wrinkle here is that people may overreport socially desirable actions in surveys, meaning these percentages are likely an overestimate. Given this, I think it’s reasonable to assume that between 10 and 40% of women buy Cruelty-Free products with some amount of intentionality, although I’d want better data to say for certain. What I can say is that Cruelty-Free cosmetics are already making waves in the beauty aisles: the Cruelty-Free market is expected to nearly double within the next ten years.

As with veganism, CF shoppers are more motivated by morals than by personal incentives. A 2025 study found that altruism — defined as an internalized concern for animal welfare, not peer pressure or social media influence — is the strongest predictor of cruelty-free purchasing behavior. Another study found that ethical concerns were a stronger predictor of cruelty-free purchases than even social norms. However, people’s ethics only drive purchases when the products are priced at or slightly above those tested on animals. It’s easy to see the overlaps with veganism, right? Ethically-driven, sometimes more expensive for an exact alternative (although, as I’ve pointed out before, vegan diets are still cheaper on average), requiring a label to buy. It’s not a perfect analogy, of course: eliminating meat consumption is harder than swapping makeup brands, and meat is far more cultural than shades of blush.

Here’s the kicker: 39% of women who only buy vegan beauty products are not actually vegan5. Another twist is that many CF shoppers don’t have a perfect understanding of what it actually entails — in one survey, only about half of participants correctly defined “cruelty-free” and “vegan” cosmetics. Taken together, this means that there is a large segment of shoppers who are buying cruelty-free products, eat a lot of meat, and may be perfect candidates for diet change.

Let’s do some back-of-the-napkin math here. If we take the percentage of shoppers who buy cruelty-free from the largest survey above (35%), multiply by the total number of potential cosmetics shoppers in the world (4.2 billion), and remove the ones who are already vegan (61%), we have: nearly 900 million people who buy cruelty-free but aren’t vegan. Heck, let’s do the math with the most conservative estimate of people who buy cruelty-free, 9%. That’s still nearly a quarter of a billion people.

Now, I’m not trying to overstate this and say that Cruelty-Free shoppers are the silver bullet we’ve been looking for6. But the success of a Cruelty-Free program means we should identify more non-diet-related behaviors that predict a smooth transition to low- or no-meat diets.

Three Kinds of Pre-Vegan We Keep Ignoring

Historically, we’ve focused on moving flexitarians through the diet-change pipeline — they’re the ones most responsive to advocacy tactics. Sometimes we’ve identified demographic characteristics that make someone more likely to go vegan, such as being left-leaning, female, or Black. But this study has made me want to reframe the question: Instead of asking “who are the right people to target?”, we should also ask “what are the right behaviors to look for?” CF cosmetics purchasing is certainly one. But how many others are there?

I’d group ideal " pre-vegans” loosely into three buckets, each defined by a different asset they already have. The first is proximity — flexitarians and vegetarians who are already partway there in their diets. Easy enough.

The second is capacity — people who’ve already demonstrated they can change an ingrained habit based on their values. Fast fashion quitters, plastic-free converts, people who’ve given up flying for climate reasons, faux fur adopters. The logic is grounded in basic behavioral psychology: people who’ve already overridden a habit for values reasons have higher confidence they can do it again — and self-efficacy is the strongest predictor of behavior change.

The third is empathy — people who already extend active moral concern to individual animals outside of diet. Here we have our shelter dog adopters, people who’ve stopped going to zoos or circuses, fair trade shoppers, and people who rescue strays. Research consistently shows that individual animal empathy is the most durable long-term predictor of sustained vegan diets.

These categories aren’t mutually exclusive: Cruelty-Free shoppers would fit into capacity and empathy buckets, for example. But it should help us broaden the idea of the vegan pipeline: we’ve historically focused almost exclusively on diet proximity, but Tu Compromiso Cruelty-Free suggests the buckets may be just as promising — and almost entirely untapped.

This also means we should expand the idea of a “diet challenge” beyond diet. They’re usually built around the assumption that diet is the entry point. But what if it isn’t? Tu Compromiso Cruelty-Free suggests the bathroom cabinet could be an entry point. There are probably many more challenge ideas out there that can be set up as funnels towards meat reduction: zero-waste challenges, fast-fashion detoxes, adopt-don’t-shop campaigns, fair-trade swap challenges, or Plastic-Free July.

What Comes Next

We know how to talk to flexitarians — heck, we’ve built entire organizations around that pipeline. We haven’t built the equivalent for the devout birdwatcher, the faux-fur convert, the man who dropped fast fashion cold turkey, the woman who religiously checks fair-trade certifications before buying chocolate. We’ve been working with a narrower definition of “pre-vegan” than the evidence supports.

We need more programs to identify these behavioral fingerprints, try new things, and help people along the routes to diet change. The data suggests it’ll work.

Thank you!

Thank you for reading! I always make these resources available for free, but please consider becoming a paid subscriber if you find my work valuable.

Subscribe now

1

Shameless plug: I’m available as a freelancer in case anyone wants me to evaluate their programs!

2

Cruelty-Free products are defined as products that don’t test on animals, while vegan cosmetics are those that don’t include animal products.

3

You may be wondering why people may sign up for a program if they are already vegan. Many of them may want to join a community, sign up with a friend, or want to learn more recipes or brands to look for. All of this is great for retention!

4

Researchy note: when I controlled for initial diet, this effect disappears, primarily because people who buy cruelty-free and people who already eat less meat overlapped substantially in my sample. This means we can’t claim that CF purchasing causes dietary change. What we can say is that CF buyers arrive with more aligned values, making them unusually strong candidates for diet-focused interventions — more so than any other factor I tested. A future round with a control group, which I hope to do this year, should help clarify the mechanism.

5

This is backed up in my Te Protejo research: about half of meat-eaters and flexitarians were Cruelty-Free but ate meat.

6

For one, Cruelty-Free consumers tend to be almost entirely women, which means its reach will always be somewhat limited, albeit more targeted.

item.title: You're Probably Thinking About Cognitive Dissonance All Wrong
item.description: The standard activist script doesn't account for what the psychological research says. Here's what does.
item.dc:creator: Björn
item.content:encoded:
Billie Eilish has made waves recently. No, I’m not talking about how she accidentally eliminated Genevieve on Survivor, but her recent comments about how people can’t love animals and also eat meat. The reaction: a verifiable outcry, exactly on cue. Cognitive dissonance right in front of our eyes.

But here’s the thing, I think lots of animal advocates are thinking about cognitive dissonance all wrong. We tend to think of it as a frustrating mental barrier – something to shake our fists at—rather than an aspect of human psychology we need to think about and navigate critically. I get it! It is frustrating seeing people advocate for suffering, or even worse, lob bigoted comments at anyone who’s actually trying to make the world a better place. But that’s not actually going to end factory farming.

Here’s my deep dive into the psychology of cognitive dissonance, and how I think we can navigate it better. The next time a musical artist makes waves like this, we need to figure out how to stop being cast as the bad guy.

What is Cognitive Dissonance Anyway?

Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort you feel when you’re holding two beliefs — or a belief and a behavior — that don’t fit together, and the mental work you do to make them gel. Like how I can maintain an extremely sophisticated cinematic palette and an unabashed love of Mean Girls. Grool.

The term comes from social psychologist Leon Festinger, who was curious after seeing doomsday cults — when the world stubbornly didn’t end, why did the members double down on their faith instead of abandoning it? In his 1957 book A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, he argued that we’re wired to reduce that internal friction, usually by taking the path of least resistance: tweaking a belief, dismissing inconvenient evidence, or quietly updating your doomsday theology so that Balazoor eats the world next year, not this year. The main takeaway is that behavior change is way harder than changing our mindset.

When it comes to meat reduction, the connection is obvious: people feel discomfort when they realize that farmed animals suffer as a direct result of their actions. The connection to meat-eating is so strong that it even has its own name: meat‐related cognitive dissonance (MRCD). As anyone who has ever seen the word “vegan” online knows, MRCD can be extremely powerful, even leading people to believe that a dietary group that makes up around 95% of the world is stigmatized itself.

How do people sort through their own MRCD? In general, through dissonance reduction, psychological or behavioral strategies to, well, reduce our dissonance. There are plenty of ways to reduce dissonance, so I plotted them all below.

How Omnivores Navigate Cognitive Dissonance:

This is a big reason why getting people to eat less meat is so hard — it is far easier to change your cognitions, especially considering that most people in the world will affirm this for you, than to change your behavior. It’s especially tricky when some studies show that even reading about a vegetarian or vegan can trigger cognitive dissonance — no finger-wagging required. Not even a vegetarian protesting or anything, just like a dude who happens to be vegetarian.

It’s not just meat-eaters. A 2023 study showed that vegetarians and pescatarians showed notably high levels of dairy/egg-related dissociation — arguably because they’re the most motivated to disconnect products they still consume from the farming practices they otherwise oppose. Another study digs in more: pescatarians actually attributed lower sentience, intelligence, and moral concern to aquatic animals than even omnivores did. Same story with dairy and eggs: both vegetarians and pescatarians rated dairy cows as less sentient and morally worthy than beef cows, and layer hens lower than broiler chickens — even though it’s literally the same animal. Our defenses track what’s on our plates, not our principles.

This shows us that while we might like to think that the poster child of cognitive dissonance is the hard-core carnivore waving barbecue tongs around like he’s about to go into battle, that’s not what the research suggests. Everyone can rationalize their way out of changing; cognitive dissonance is slippier than it might seem.

Men and women experience cognitive dissonance differently — a 2018 experimental study found that when participants were exposed to information about the animal origins of their food, women experienced significantly more negative emotions and decreased attachment to meat, while men’s feelings barely budged. More telling: men’s attachment to meat actually increased when confronted with the meat-animal connection — a defensive doubling-down that will surprise no one who has ever argued about this at a dinner table. The underlying pattern makes psychological sense. Women tend to manage the meat paradox through dissociation — mentally separating the pork chop from the pig — which means that when that strategy is blocked by a visual reminder, they feel the discomfort more acutely. Men, meanwhile, tend to respond to the same challenge by digging in.

The standard activist move — point out the contradiction and let guilt take the wheel — is already a fairly blunt instrument. For many people, particularly men, the data suggest it can actually backfire.

How We Should Change Our Advocacy

I often find that vegan activists use cognitive dissonance more like gotcha journalists than therapists: springing out to point out hypocrisies instead of thinking critically about how to approach a complicated mental concept. I’m guilty of this myself! But I don’t think that’s helpful — we’re too focused on critiquing its existence after-the-fact instead of trying to navigate it correctly before it occurs. Here are three ways to approach it better:

First, think critically about the order of the conversation.

This is probably the most important thing: avoiding having these conversations after someone eats meat. In one study, participants were assigned to eat either cashews or beef jerky and then complete a series of tasks seemingly unrelated to the snack. One of those tasks turned out to be identifying the moral value of certain animals, including a cow. The people who ate beef jerky rated the cow as less deserving of moral worth than the people who munched on cashews. In other words, eating meat makes people value animals less, at least in the immediate aftermath of their meal.

Another study took it further. They had participants write about cows and sheep in front of either a bowl of apples or “an appetizingly presented delicatessen roast beef/lamb infused with rosemary and garlic.” The folks who rated the farmed animals in front of their meat were more likely to say those animals had limited mental capabilities than those who did it in front of a fruit basket.

So the data is clear on what to avoid — but the flip side is just as important: when should you have this conversation? The answer isn’t just “not after a meal.” I’d argued it’s after someone has already done something positive. If someone is halfway through Veganuary, has just called their representative about the Farm Bill (please do this), or tried out a new plant-based restaurant, they’re more likely to want to have this conversation. Action precedes openness.

Timing, though, is only half of it. The induced hypocrisy paradigm, developed from Festinger’s original theory and now backed by several decades of empirical research, flips the standard activist script. Instead of confronting someone with their contradiction, you ask them to voice a value they already hold, and then — privately, not publicly — invite them to notice where their behavior falls short. It’s been applied to condom use, recycling, discrimination, and blood donation with consistent effects. Start by asking what they value — do they like animals, do they care about sustainability? Then, privately, invite them to consider whether their actions line up. I know it sounds like therapy-speak, but lots of organizations already use this idea in their conversations and messaging!

The underlying logic — meet people where their values already are — has been tested directly in animal advocacy contexts. One study at a zoo found that a message reading “Do you consider animal welfare to be important?” above a veggie burger doubled its orders compared to a control, from 5% to 10%. I mean, that’s still pretty low for a place that claims to be all about loving animals, but I digress.

For animal advocates, the implication is counterintuitive but clear: the conversation that changes behavior probably starts with you asking someone what they believe about animals, not telling them what you think of their diet.

Second, validate and affirm the person’s agency and morality.

A landmark study across 89 countries during COVID-19 found that autonomy-supportive messaging (language that emphasizes choice and personal agency instead of obligation) reduced stubbornness toward social distancing compared with controlling or shame-based appeals. If you’ve ever heard someone say that vegans are “shoving things down my throat,” this probably feels familiar to you. The practical translation is simple: lead with options, not imperatives. “Here are some ways people are reducing their consumption” lands a bit better than “you need to stop eating meat.”

While you’re at it, you should probably uplift the person as well — according to self-affirmation theory, people respond far less defensively to threatening messages when they’ve first been reminded of who they are at their best. You may be saying “farmed animals are suffering” or “meat is murder,” but they might be hearing “you think I’m a bad person.” Try something more like “I know you’re trying to do the right thing here, I see it.1”

Third: when all else fails, change the ask.

There probably comes a point in certain advocacy conversations when you realize the other person isn’t changing their diet today, this year, or possibly ever. That doesn’t mean the conversation is wasted. Consider shifting the ask to something easier — voting for pro-environmental or pro-animal politicians, donating to animal welfare organizations or alternative protein companies, or supporting other meat-reduction policies, like plant-based defaults or meat taxes. This is arguably the better play regardless: the meat reduction movement is egregiously underfunded, and collective action through policy and funding may be more important in the long run.

The Bottom Line

The next time a pop star says something about animals and the internet catches fire, everyone who cares about this issue will face a choice: join the pile-on and get the dopamine hit of being publicly right (again, I’m calling myself out here too), or actually try to use the moment. Cognitive dissonance is a feature of the human brain, not a bug — it’s not going anywhere, but it is navigable. So instead of catching someone mid-burger and hoping guilt does the rest, we should try asking before telling, meeting people where their values already are, and knowing when to change the ask entirely.

Billie Eilish isn’t the first person to place the meat paradox firmly into the news cycle, and she won’t be the last. The question is whether we get any better at this.
